title: Optimization and efficiency strategies demonstrate fuel savings while maximizing science collection on a fishery survey
content:
Abstract
Optimizing the energy budget of oceanographic research vessels is critical to maintaining scientific capacity due to fuel cost volatility and limited days at sea. Standard commercial efficiency strategies, such as speed reduction (“slow steaming”), often reduce scientific productivity when applied to research platforms dominated by high fixed “hotel loads” (i.e. total electrical power consumed except for propulsion). This study quantifies the operational efficiency of a fishery research vessel during annual mid-water trawl surveys (2021–2025) to identify drivers of fuel consumption and evaluate optimization strategies. By integrating daily engineering logs with time-corrected, high-resolution vessel tracking, we utilized regression analysis to partition fuel consumption into fixed base loads and variable propulsion costs. Results reveal a trend towards improvement in fuel efficiency (~13.6 to 15.6%), with fuel intensity declining from a baseline of 35.13 liters per nautical mile in 2021 to 30.36 liters in 2025. Survey simulations demonstrated that capping transit speeds at either 8 or 9 knots, while theoretically lowering daily consumption, resulted in an unacceptable loss of survey coverage, effectively increasing the fuel cost per unit of data collected. Instead, the observed savings were attributed to a base load management strategy (a single-generator transit protocol) which structurally reduced daily fuel demand without compromising vessel speed or scientific data density. We conclude that maximizing scientific yield requires maintaining efficient transit speeds while utilizing collaborative engineering protocols to minimize hotel loads, offering a scalable framework for cost avoidance across similar research vessels and fishery surveys. We offer this scalable framework as food for thought to stimulate a cross-disciplinary dialogue on the sustainable future of oceanographic observation and fishery science.
